categories: ["การติดเชื้อราที่ผิวหนัง"]
synonyms: ["Dermatophytosis", "Fungal Skin Infection", "Ringworm", "Skin Tinea", "Tinea Corporis", "Tinea Infection", "Pityriasis versicolor"]
conventional_description:
Tinea is a common fungal infection of the skin, hair, or nails caused by dermatophytes - a group of fungi that feed on keratin. It can appear anywhere on the body: the feet (athlete's foot), groin (jock itch), scalp, or trunk (ringworm). The classic sign is a red, scaly, ring-shaped rash with a clearer center, often accompanied by itching, burning, or cracking.
Diagnosis is usually made by looking at the rash, but a doctor may take a skin scraping for a KOH test or culture to confirm the fungus. Tinea thrives in warm, moist environments and spreads easily through direct contact or contaminated surfaces like locker-room floors.
conventional_treatments: Most cases are treated with topical antifungal creams, sprays, or powders that directly kill the fungus. For widespread or stubborn infections, oral antifungal medications like terbinafine or fluconazole may be prescribed. Keeping the skin clean and dry is also recommended to prevent recurrence.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, tinea is understood as an invasion of external pathogens - primarily Dampness, Heat, and Wind - that lodge in the skin. But these pathogens can only take hold when there's an internal weakness. The Spleen is often at the center of the story: when it's too weak to transform fluids properly, Dampness accumulates inside the body, creating a sticky, humid environment that mirrors the warm, moist conditions fungi love.
This internal Dampness can then combine with Heat, either from a feverish constitution or from spicy, greasy foods, and the two together pour downward or spread outward to the skin.
The location of the rash gives important clues. When damp-heat sinks to the lower burner, it typically shows up as athlete's foot with weeping, macerated skin between the toes. When it affects the Spleen more broadly, the rash may appear on the trunk or groin and come with bloating, nausea, and a heavy sensation. In both cases, the skin is moist and inflamed - the perfect breeding ground for fungus.
Chronic, long-standing tinea tells a different story. Here, the body's Blood and fluids have become depleted, often from prolonged illness, poor diet, or aging. Without enough nourishment, the skin turns dry, scaly, and thickened. This dryness generates internal Wind, which combines with external Wind to cause intense itching that gets worse at night.
In some stubborn cases, the lingering pathogens damage the Blood so deeply that it congeals and stagnates, turning the lesions dark, fixed, and resistant to treatment.
What looks like one fungal infection to a dermatologist can actually be five different internal landscapes to a TCM practitioner - each requiring a different combination of herbs, acupuncture points, and lifestyle shifts to truly clear the skin and prevent recurrence.
classical_quote: 「癣者，风湿邪气，客于腠理，复值寒湿，与血气相搏，则血气否涩，发此疾也。」
classical_translation: "Tinea is caused by wind and dampness evil qi lodging in the interstices of the skin, combined with cold and dampness, which contend with the blood and qi, causing stagnation of blood and qi, thus giving rise to this disease."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by examining the skin lesion closely - its color, moisture, thickness, and distribution - and asks about the onset, triggers, and accompanying symptoms. The location is also key: foot involvement often points downward, while widespread body lesions may reflect internal organ imbalances.
If the lesion is moist, with vesicles, maceration, and oozing, and the person complains of intense itching, a red tongue with a thick yellow greasy coating, and a slippery, rapid pulse, the pattern is likely Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. This is very common in athlete’s foot, where heat and dampness pour downward.
When similar damp-heat signs appear on the trunk or groin and are accompanied by digestive issues like bloating, loose stools, or a heavy sensation in the body, the pattern is Damp-Heat invading the Spleen. The tongue coating is greasy, and the pulse is soft or slippery, reflecting Spleen dysfunction failing to transform fluids.
Chronic, long-standing tinea that presents with dry, thickened, scaly plaques and cracks, and itching that worsens at night, suggests Blood Deficiency with External Wind. Here the tongue is pale with little coating, and the pulse is fine. The skin is undernourished, and wind from dryness stirs the itching.
When lesions are persistent, dark red or purple, infiltrated, and do not fade with treatment, Blood Stagnation is present. The tongue may be purple with stasis spots, and the pulse is choppy. This pattern often underlies stubborn, recurrent infections.
An acute flare with bright red, inflamed, rapidly spreading patches and a rapid pulse points to Heat in the Blood. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coat. This can occur alone or alongside damp-heat, indicating a more aggressive inflammatory response.

patterns.worse_with: Hot, humid weather, Sweating or damp shoes, Greasy, spicy, or sweet foods, Alcohol and coffee
patterns.better_with: Keeping skin dry, Cool, dry environment, Breathable cotton socks, Avoiding damp public floors
patterns.why_this_happens:
When external dampness and heat invade the body, or when the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, damp-heat accumulates and sinks to the lower burner. This pathogenic damp-heat settles in the skin of the feet, toes, and groin, creating a moist, hot environment that encourages fungal overgrowth.
The dampness causes the skin to weep, macerate, and form blisters, while the heat drives intense itching, redness, and a foul odor. The condition often worsens in warm, humid weather, which further fuels the damp-heat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, greasy yellow coating that is most prominent at the root. Pulse: slippery and rapid, often more pronounced at the rear (Chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat pathogens thrive in moist, warm conditions, so hot, humid weather and sweaty feet worsen the condition. Greasy, spicy foods and alcohol generate internal dampness and heat, fueling the skin lesions. Keeping the skin dry and cool starves the damp-heat, while breathable fabrics prevent moisture buildup.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, spicy, and sugary foods that generate internal dampness and heat. Keep feet clean and dry; wear breathable cotton socks and change them daily. Choose well-ventilated shoes and avoid walking barefoot in damp public areas like locker rooms. Limit alcohol and rich, heavy meals.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable energy and moisture. When it becomes sluggish-often from a diet heavy in greasy or sweet foods-it fails to manage moisture properly, allowing internal Dampness to accumulate. Over time this Dampness combines with Heat, and the resulting Damp-Heat overflows into the skin, producing the oozing blisters and intense itching typical of tinea. The digestive symptoms like bloating, nausea, and sticky stools are a direct sign that the Spleen is struggling.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow, greasy coating thickest at the centre and root; may be swollen with teeth marks. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), or slippery (Hua) and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and sweet foods directly overwhelm the Spleen, creating more Damp-Heat that the body then pushes out through the skin. A light, bland diet and a dry environment reduce that burden, allowing the Spleen to recover and clear the dampness. Stress knots the Liver Qi, which further impairs the Spleen’s function, so calming habits and gentle movement help restore the smooth flow that keeps Dampness from accumulating.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and heavily sweetened foods-they generate Damp-Heat. Base meals around lightly cooked grains, vegetables, and small amounts of lean protein; congee with barley (Yi Yi Ren) is especially helpful. Keep the skin clean and dry, wear loose, breathable clothing, and limit alcohol. Gentle daily movement like walking helps the Spleen’s Qi move and clears Dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Blood is insufficient, the skin loses its nourishment and becomes dry, scaly, and thickened. This dryness generates internal Wind, which combines with external Wind invading from the environment, causing the characteristic itching that comes and goes and worsens at night. In chronic tinea, this pattern leads to persistent, dry, cracked patches rather than the weeping, red lesions of acute damp-heat patterns.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white, slightly dry coating. Pulse: fine (thin), wiry on the left guan (Liver) position, and floating on the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Deficiency means the skin is undernourished and prone to dryness and Wind. Moisturizers and nourishing foods replenish Blood and fluids, calming internal Wind, while wind exposure directly triggers external Wind invasion - the very mechanism of this pattern. Stress and overwork consume Blood and Qi, worsening the deficiency; gentle movement and rest help preserve Blood and promote circulation without draining it. Spicy and drying foods generate internal Heat and consume fluids, aggravating dryness and itching. By choosing moistening, blood-building foods and protecting the skin from harsh environments, the body can gradually restore its Blood and expel lingering Wind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat blood-nourishing foods like bone broth, eggs, dark leafy greens, black sesame, and small amounts of red meat. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that deplete fluids. Keep skin well-moisturized with natural creams, and protect yourself from drafts and cold, dry wind. Gentle daily movement like walking helps circulate Blood without exhausting it.

The stagnant blood blocks the channels, leading to stabbing pain that is worse at night and with pressure, and the rash becomes stubborn and resistant to treatment.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with possible stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩, sè) or wiry (弦, xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold congeals blood, so warmth and movement help it flow. Stress and frustration stagnate Liver Qi, which in turn worsens blood stasis. Nighttime is when blood circulation naturally slows, making pain and itching more noticeable. Greasy foods can generate dampness and hinder circulation. Blood-moving spices and gentle exercise directly counter stagnation, while avoiding pressure prevents further blockage in the channels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, black vinegar, and small amounts of red meat. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks that congeal the blood. Gentle daily exercise such as walking or stretching helps keep Qi and blood flowing. Keep the skin clean and dry, but avoid harsh soaps that dry the skin further. Warm compresses on the lesions can ease pain and itching.

patterns.why_this_happens: Heat in the Blood is an acute, deep-level imbalance where excess heat penetrates beyond the surface into the blood itself. When this happens, the blood becomes agitated and overheated, pushing inflammation outward to the skin. In tinea, this manifests as a sudden flare of bright red, angry-looking patches that may appear rapidly and spread quickly. The heat also consumes the body's cooling fluids, making the skin feel burning and intensely itchy, and can even cause small bleeding points or oozing within the rash.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red spots or prickles, thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: rapid (shu) and wiry (xian), possibly slippery (hua), with force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat in the Blood is a true excess heat pattern. Any external or internal heat-spicy food, alcohol, hot environments, or emotional fire-adds fuel to the fire, intensifying the redness, burning, and spread. Cooling measures literally draw heat out of the blood, while rest and calm prevent the agitation that stirs the blood further. The goal is to cool the blood back down so the skin can heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid all heating foods and drinks: alcohol, coffee, spicy dishes, lamb, and deep-fried foods. Embrace cooling, hydrating foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and chrysanthemum tea. Keep the affected skin clean and dry, but avoid hot showers or scrubbing. Rest is essential; overexertion or emotional stress can fan the internal heat.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure ringworm?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can resolve tinea infections by correcting the internal imbalances that allow the fungus to thrive. Herbal formulas and external washes work together to clear Dampness, Heat, and Wind while nourishing the skin. For many people, this approach not only clears the current rash but also reduces the likelihood of recurrence, which is a common frustration with conventional antifungals alone.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture help with fungal skin infections?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture doesn't kill the fungus directly, but it can be a powerful support. By strengthening the Spleen to transform Dampness, clearing Heat from the blood, or moving stagnant Blood, acupuncture helps change the internal environment that sustains the infection. Points like Spleen 9 (Yinlingquan) and Stomach 36 (Zusanli) are often used to drain dampness, while Blood-moving points address chronic, thickened plaques. It's usually combined with herbal medicine for the best results.

faqs.question: How long does TCM treatment take for athlete's foot?
faqs.answer: For a typical acute case of athlete's foot with weeping and itching, you may see significant improvement in 2-4 weeks with daily herbal soaks and internal formulas. If the infection has been present for months or years and the skin is dry and cracked, it may take 2-3 months to fully rebuild the skin's health. Your practitioner will adjust the treatment as the rash changes.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my antifungal cream?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Topical antifungal creams and TCM external washes can often be used at different times of day - just leave a gap of a few hours to avoid interaction. If you're taking oral antifungal medication, always tell both your doctor and your TCM practitioner, as some herbs may affect liver function and could interact with drugs like terbinafine. Never stop a prescribed medication without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have tinea?
faqs.answer: In TCM, foods that create Dampness and Heat are the main culprits. This includes greasy, fried, and overly sweet foods, dairy products, alcohol, and rich meats. Instead, favor cooling, drying foods like barley, mung beans, bitter greens, and lightly cooked vegetables. Keeping your diet simple and clean helps starve the fungus of its preferred internal environment.

faqs.question: Is tinea contagious from a TCM perspective?
faqs.answer: TCM recognizes that external pathogens - including the fungal element - can spread through direct contact. However, whether you catch it depends on your internal strength. A person with strong Qi and no internal Dampness is far less susceptible, even when exposed. This is why some family members never get it while others struggle with repeated infections. TCM focuses on strengthening your terrain so the fungus can't take hold.

faqs.question: Will the rash come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Recurrence is much less likely when the underlying pattern is fully corrected. If only the surface symptoms were treated - for example, with an external wash alone - the rash may return when conditions are right. A complete TCM approach addresses both the skin and the internal imbalance, which significantly lowers the chance of the infection coming back. Your practitioner will guide you on how long to continue treatment to prevent relapse.

research.title: Therapeutic Evaluation of Herbal Foot Bath for Tinea Pedis
research.description: A randomized controlled trial evaluating a multi-herb foot soak (including Sophora flavescens, Phellodendron amurense, and Kochia scoparia) for tinea pedis. The herbal group showed significant reduction in itching, scaling, and erythema compared to placebo, with a higher mycological cure rate and lower recurrence at follow-up.
research.periodical: Therapeutic Evaluation of Herbal Foot Bath for Tinea Pedis. Pakistan Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences. 2025.

research.title: Efficacy and active components of herbal extracts on the treatment of dermatophytosis
research.description: A laboratory and clinical study investigating herbal extracts against common dermatophytes. The formula containing Sophora flavescens and Cassia twig demonstrated strong antifungal activity in vitro and, in a small clinical cohort, improved symptoms of tinea corporis and tinea cruris with minimal side effects.
research.periodical: Efficacy and active components of herbal extracts on the treatment of dermatophytosis. Hong Kong Medical Journal. 2005;11(Suppl 2):44.
